title: Senior's toolkit: interfaces, navigation and DI lifetimes
summary: Extract interfaces, find every caller and implementation, and register dependencies with the right lifetime.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: interfaces, navigation and DI lifetimes
steps.body: SOLID at work is mostly done with the IDE and the dependency injection container: find who depends on what, pull an interface out, and register the implementation with a lifetime that will not bite you in production.

toolkit.what: Find all references: every caller of a method or user of a type. Run it before you change a signature, so you know the blast radius.
toolkit.when: before changing or splitting a class others depend on

toolkit.what: Go to implementation: jump from an interface or abstract member to the classes that implement it. F12 alone lands on the interface, which is rarely what you want.
Generate an interface from a class's public members and make the class implement it. The first step of inverting a dependency.
flags: Visual Studio and VS Code: Extract interface...
Rider: Refactor This, then Extract Interface
include only what callers need (interface segregation)
toolkit.example: Ctrl+. on class SmtpMailer, Extract interface, name it IMailer, tick Send only

toolkit.what: Register an implementation for an interface in ASP.NET Core's container. Classes ask for `IPayrollStore` in their constructor and never `new` the concrete type.
flags: one instance for the whole app; must be thread-safe
one instance per request (per scope); the norm for DbContext and units of work
a new instance every time it is asked for

toolkit.cmd: public sealed class PayrollService(IPayrollStore store, TimeProvider clock)
toolkit.what: Constructor injection with a C# 12 primary constructor. The dependencies are visible in one line, and a long list is a sign the class does too much.
flags: parameters are in scope in the whole class body
says the class is not designed for inheritance

toolkit.what: Container checks that fail at start-up on a missing registration or a scoped service captured by a singleton. On by default in the Development environment; turn them on everywhere if start-up time allows.
flags: construct-check every registration when the app starts
refuse to resolve a scoped service from the root or from a singleton

toolkit.what: Register only if nobody registered that service yet (namespace `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Extensions`). Libraries use it for defaults the app can override.
flags: no-op when the service type is already registered
adds another registration; the last one wins for single resolves

steps.prompt: Match each lifetime to what the container does.
pairs: one instance shared by the whole app
a new instance on every resolve

steps.prompt: The app refuses to start in Development with this error. What is the design problem?
code: System.AggregateException: Some services are not able to be constructed
(Error while validating the service descriptor 'ServiceType: IPayslipCache Lifetime: Singleton
ImplementationType: PayslipCache': Cannot consume scoped service 'PayrollDbContext' from singleton 'IPayslipCache'.)
options: A singleton holds a scoped DbContext, so one context would be shared by every request; make the cache scoped or have it create a scope (or use `IDbContextFactory`) when it needs the database
The error only happens in Development, so it is safe to ignore in production
steps.explain: This is a captive dependency. In production, without the check, the singleton would keep the first request's DbContext forever: stale data and thread-safety bugs. The check exists to catch it at start-up.

steps.prompt: Register the store once per request and the system clock once for the whole app.
steps.explain: A store that wraps a DbContext follows the request scope. `TimeProvider.System` is one shared, thread-safe instance, so it is a singleton; only the singleton overload takes a ready-made instance.

steps.prompt: Which IDE action answers the question?
items: Who calls `Payroll.Calculate` before I change its signature?
Where is the real code behind `store.SaveAsync` in this constructor-injected class?
`ReportService` news up `SmtpMailer` and I want to swap it in tests
Callers only need `Send` from a class with 12 public methods

steps.prompt: `ReportService` creates `new SmtpMailer()` inside a method. Put the steps of inverting that dependency in order.
lines: Shift+F12 on SmtpMailer to see who creates and uses it
Extract interface IMailer from SmtpMailer with only Send
Take IMailer as a constructor parameter of ReportService instead of calling new
Run the tests, then add one that passes a fake IMailer

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before you change a class, press Shift+F12 and read who depends on it. When you see `new` of something that talks to the outside world, extract an interface and inject it. Pick the lifetime on purpose, and keep scope validation on so a captive dependency fails at start-up instead of in production.
